cite.paraphrase: Wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is that by which one sees wrongly, or which sees wrongly, or mere wrong seeing: its mark is unwise insistence; its function is clinging; its manifestation is wrong adherence; its proximate cause is the wish not to see the noble ones and the like; it is to be regarded as the most blameworthy. Restlessness (uddhacca) is agitated state: its mark is non-calming; its function is unsteadiness, like water stirred by wind; its manifestation is bewilderment, like a flag fluttering in the wind or like ashes thrown up by a blow on a stone; its proximate cause is unwise attention to the non-calming of the mind; it is to be regarded as distraction of consciousness. The other factors are as stated for the unwholesome. The second unwholesome consciousness is like the first, but prompted and with sloth-torpor indeterminate. Sloth (thīna) is the sinking, torpor (middha) the drowsing: sloth has as its mark lack of energy and as function dispelling energy, as manifestation sinking; torpor has as mark unworkableness, as function smothering, as manifestation drooping or drowsy sleep; for both the proximate cause is unwise attention to discontent, lazy stretching and the like. Conceit (māna), indeterminate in the third and fourth, has as mark haughtiness, as function self-promotion, as manifestation vain-glory, as proximate cause greed dissociated from view; it is to be regarded as madness. The fifth to eighth are given in the same manner without wrong view or with joy left out.

cite.paraphrase: At the moment of the arahat path he emerges from the remaining fetters and latent tendencies (from lust for fine-material and immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness, ignorance; the latent conceit, latent lust for existence, latent ignorance), from the defilements that follow them and the aggregates, and outwardly from all signs: as quoted, "understanding in the turning away by emerging in both ways is knowledge in the path". In the development of the eight worldly attainments calm is stronger; in developing the contemplation of impermanence and so on, insight is stronger; in the moment of the noble path they occur yoked together, neither exceeding the other; so in the four knowledges of the paths there is a joining of both powers. The text quotes the Paṭisambhidā: for one emerging from the defilements accompanied by restlessness and from the aggregates, one-pointedness of mind, non-distraction, is concentration whose domain is cessation; for one emerging from the defilements accompanied by ignorance, insight in the sense of contemplation has cessation as domain; thus in the sense of emerging calm and insight are of one taste, yoked and not exceeding each other. Then, under "what is to be abandoned by which, and the abandoning", the text begins: in these four knowledges one should know what states are to be abandoned by each knowledge, states that come as fetters, defilements, wrongnesses, worldly conditions, avarice, perversions, ties, wrong courses, taints, floods, yokes, hindrances, adherences, clingings, latent tendencies, stains, unwholesome courses of action and unwholesome thoughts. Fetters are ten things that bind beings to aggregates, to the fruit of kamma and to suffering; of them five are higher fetters (lust for fine-material existence, for immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness, ignorance) (continued on p. 683).

duḥkham ādhyātmikam ādhibhautikam ādhidaivikaṃ ca /

cite.paraphrase: Pain (duḥkha) is of three kinds: relating to oneself (ādhyātmika), to other beings (ādhibhautika), and to the divine (ādhidaivika); it is that by which beings are struck and strive to strike it down. Dejection (daurmanasya) is a disturbance (kṣobha) of the mind through the frustration of a wish. Trembling of the limbs (aṅgamejayatva) is that which shakes the limbs. Inhalation (śvāsa) is when the vital breath (prāṇa) takes in outer air; exhalation (praśvāsa) is when it expels air from the belly. These are companions of distraction: they occur in one whose mind is distracted (vikṣipta); they do not occur in one whose mind is concentrated (samāhita).

statement: Your words “i want to go straight back to it” fit only loosely what the Jain texts call Ārta-dhyāna (sorrowful dwelling). Meditation (dhyāna) is of four kinds: sorrowful (ārta), cruel (raudra), virtuous (dharmya) and pure (śukla) (TS 9.28); the last two are causes of liberation (TS 9.29).

cite.title: Tattvārthasūtra
cite.paraphrase: Dhyāna is of four kinds: ārta (pained), raudra (fierce), dharmya (of dharma) and śukla (white).

cite.paraphrase: Contemplation of mind (citta). The Buddha asks how a monk abides contemplating mind in mind. Here he knows a mind with lust (sarāga) as 'mind with lust', and a mind without lust as 'mind without lust'; a mind with hatred (sadosa) and without hatred; a mind with delusion (samoha) and without delusion; a contracted (saṅkhitta) mind and a scattered (vikkhitta) mind; an exalted (mahaggata) and an unexalted mind; a surpassable (sauttara) and an unsurpassable (anuttara) mind; a concentrated (samāhita) and an unconcentrated mind; a liberated (vimutta) and an unliberated mind.

statement: For what you wrote, “i want to go straight back to it”: (1) Daurmanasya in YS is a companion of distraction: it occurs in a distracted mind and is absent in a concentrated one (YB 1.31). (2) Arjuna's viṣāda is a crisis about dharma, and it becomes the occasion of the whole teaching (BhG 2.7). (3) Jain ārta-dhyāna is a kind of meditation (dhyāna), the inauspicious sorrowful one of four (TS 9.28): a sustained fixing of the mind, not a passing mood. This row describes states the texts name. It is not a finding about any person, and it makes no health claim.

yas tv ekāgre cetasi sadbhūtam arthaṃ pradyotayati kṣiṇoti ca kleśān karmabandhanāni ślathayati nirodham abhimukhaṃ karoti sa saṃprajñāto yoga ity ākhyāyate /
sa ca vitarkānugato vicārānugata ānandānugato 'smitānugata ity upariṣṭān nivedayiṣyāmaḥ /
sarvavṛttinirodhe tv asaṃprajñātaḥ samādhiḥ
cite.paraphrase: 'Now' (atha) marks that a topic is taken up (adhikāra): the treatise called 'the teaching of yoga' is to be understood as the subject in hand. Yoga is samādhi, and samādhi is a property of the mind (citta) at every level (sārvabhauma). The levels of the mind (citta-bhūmi) are: scattered (kṣipta), stupefied (mūḍha), distracted (vikṣipta), one-pointed (ekāgra) and stilled (niruddha). In a distracted mind, samādhi that has become subordinate to the distraction does not count on the side of yoga. But in the one-pointed mind, the samādhi that illumines the real object (sadbhūta artha), wears away the afflictions (kleśa), loosens the bonds of karma and turns the mind toward stilling (nirodha) is called samprajñāta yoga. That samādhi is accompanied by reasoning (vitarka), by reflection (vicāra), by joy (ānanda) or by I-am-ness (asmitā) — Vyāsa says he will set this out later. In the stilling of all activities, samādhi is asamprajñāta.
